title: Global Survey Finds 90% of Quantum Companies Rely on Cross-Border Supply Chains - Quantum Computing Report
gist: A multi-consortium Global Quantum Supply Chain Flows report (QED-C, QuIC, QIC, UKQuantum, Q-STAR, KQIA, QURECA) surveying 160 quantum firms in 15 countries finds 90% depend on at least one foreign supplier and 74% sell abroad, making national protectionist trade controls a direct risk to the sector. Component suppliers (cryogenics, photonics, control electronics) have broader export reach than full-system QPU makers.

insights.claim: A survey of 160 quantum enterprises headquartered in 15 countries found that 90% rely on at least one foreign supplier for specialized hardware components or software, with a median of 3 supplier countries.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
entities: Global Quantum Supply Chain Flows report
insights.so_what: Near-universal foreign sourcing means quantum firms are exposed to any tariff or export-control escalation between allied and non-allied states.
insights.quote: 90% of quantum companies rely on at least one foreign supplier for specialized hardware components or software

insights.claim: 74% of surveyed quantum companies serve commercial customers abroad (median of 3 customer countries), and respondents collectively export to 49 customer countries, source from 36 supplier countries, and manufacture across 25 countries.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Quantum company revenue scaling depends on foreign market access, so export restrictions would hit top lines as well as input costs.

insights.claim: Quantum supply chains rely heavily on international sources of cryogenics, lasers, and control electronics, and even micro-SMEs with 1–9 employees require cross-border supplier networks.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Early-stage quantum startups carry supply-chain geopolitical risk from day one; diligence should map their critical component origins.
insights.locator: Global Quantum Supply Chain Flows 2026 Key Survey Benchmarks

insights.claim: The top geographic hubs of the quantum supply chain are the United States, Germany, the United Kingdom, Canada, and Japan, and the European Union taken as a bloc is the second-largest hub.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: US-EU trade relations are the single most important corridor for quantum supply chain continuity.
insights.locator: Global Quantum Supply Chain Flows 2026 Key Survey Benchmarks

insights.claim: Quantum component suppliers (cryogenics, photonics, control electronics, specialized materials) report broader geographic export reach than full-system QPU developers, reflecting that end-user quantum computers are still pre-commercial while subsystem manufacturing is mature.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Picks-and-shovels component suppliers currently monetize the quantum build-out more broadly than QPU developers, a possible lower-risk exposure to the sector.
insights.quote: reflecting the pre-commercial state of end-user quantum computing hardware relative to mature subsystem manufacturing
insights.locator: The report highlights that quantum component suppliers

insights.claim: Policymakers pursuing national protectionist trade controls on quantum technology face a direct tension because such controls risk disrupting access to critical international deep-tech suppliers that nearly all quantum firms depend on.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Watch for quantum-specific export control rules; unilateral controls could raise costs and delay roadmaps for hardware developers.
insights.quote: tension facing policymakers attempting to implement national protectionist trade controls without disrupting access to critical international deep-tech suppliers

insights.claim: Industry consortia leaders from QED-C, QuIC, UKQuantum, QIC, KQIA, and QURECA argue that technology sovereignty and economic security require allied nations to build multilateral frameworks that keep trusted trade channels open while protecting sensitive dual-use quantum technologies.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Industry is lobbying for allied 'trusted trade' blocs rather than national controls; policy outcomes will shape which firms keep global market access.
insights.locator: Industry leaders from QED-C, QuIC, UKQuantum
